chapters.title: 7.1 Cookies, Local Storage, Session Storage
chapters.overviewText: Since Cypress 12, cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage are cleared between tests — and in-memory app state dies because the page itself resets to about:blank. Treat every it() as a blank browser unless you opt into cy.session() or { testIsolation: false }. Storage is origin-scoped; cy.origin() state is invisible outside that origin. clearAllCookies/getAllLocalStorage exist for whole-browser visibility.
chapters.why: The classic 'login test then a second it() that assumes still logged in' bug is isolation working as designed, not a Cypress defect. Knowing v12+ clears all stores — not just cookies — stops you from cargo-culting old cy.clearLocalStorage() tutorials.
chapters.when: When a second test in a spec is redirected to /login, when debugging auth with cy.getCookies(), or when SSO spans two origins.

practical.scenario: it('logs in') then it('views approvals') in the same describe, no beforeEach.
practical.pass: You put cy.loginAs('manager') in beforeEach (cached in 7.2) so each test establishes its own state.
practical.fail: You disable isolation to make the second test pass, or assume cookies survived because they survive cy.reload().

chapters.customSummary:
- This chapter's question, distinct from Part 3.10's mechanics: what actually persists across a test boundary, and what silently vanishes?
- Cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage are all cleared between tests (v12+) — and so is in-memory JS application state (Redux/React state), because Cypress doesn't just clear storage, it resets the page itself
- Mental model: treat every it() as starting from a blank browser, with two deliberate, opt-in exceptions — cy.session() (restores from a cache, 7.2) and { testIsolation: false } (disables the reset for a whole suite, 7.3). Absent either, assume nothing survives
- This directly prevents the classic bug of a "login" test and a "do something while logged in" test being split across two it() blocks assuming shared state — the fix is making every test independently establish what it needs via beforeEach + cached login, not fighting the reset
- Storage is origin-scoped by browser design, not a Cypress choice — state set inside a cy.origin() block (Part 9.1) is invisible outside that origin, exactly as for a real user. clearAllCookies()/getAllLocalStorage() (v12+) exist specifically for whole-browser, cross-origin visibility
- Inspecting storage/cookies via cy.log() mid-test is a legitimate, fast first diagnostic step for state-smelling failures, before reaching for heavier tools (Part 12.1)
- vs Playwright: storageState makes "what persists" an explicit, serializable file artifact from the start, rather than something reasoned about via hook placement. vs Selenium: no isolation policy at all — a WebDriver session's cookie jar persists until manually cleared, making Selenium suites more exposed to accidental cross-test leakage by default than Cypress's stricter default

chapters.title: 7.2 cy.session() for Login Caching
chapters.overviewText: cy.session(name, setupFn) runs setup once per key, snapshots cookies and storage, and restores them later without re-running login. validate() re-checks before restore and re-runs setup on failure. cacheAcrossSpecs: true amortizes one login across every spec in a cypress run. After session, Cypress navigates to about:blank — always follow with cy.visit(). Setup can be API or full UI; you pay the real cost exactly once.
chapters.why: Isolation and performance pull against each other; cy.session() is the sanctioned exception to 'assume nothing persists.' Forgetting the follow-up visit is the most common first-time bug. Playwright storageState persists across CLI invocations; Cypress's cache does not.
chapters.when: Implementing cy.loginAs, switching employee/manager mid-spec, or caching an SSO UI login that has no API bypass.

practical.scenario: A spec needs employee (no approve button) then manager (approve exists), plus 40 other specs that also need manager.
practical.pass: You cy.session(role, ...) with validate against /api/auth/me, cacheAcrossSpecs: true, then cy.visit after each restore.
practical.fail: You set localStorage in the test body (wiped next test), skip validate, or forget cy.visit and assert against about:blank.

chapters.customSummary:
- Reconciles isolation (fresh state every test) with performance (don't pay the login cost every test) — caches the result of an auth flow (cookies + storage), keyed by a name, and restores it without re-running the setup logic
- Basic shape: cy.session(name, setupFn) — setupFn runs in full only the first time for a given key; every later call restores the snapshot instead
- State set inside the setupFn (e.g. window.localStorage.setItem(...)) is captured in the snapshot — this is specifically the sanctioned exception to 7.1's "assume nothing persists," unlike setting storage as a bare step in a test body
- validate() is what makes the cache trustworthy over a long run: re-checked every time a cached session is about to be restored; on failure, Cypress transparently discards the cache and reruns setupFn fresh — turns "silently stale session" into a self-healing non-issue
- cacheAcrossSpecs: true extends the cache across every spec file in one cypress run invocation, not just within one file — the first spec pays the cost once for the whole run
- Sessions are keyed by the name/object argument — different roles get independent caches automatically, and switching between them mid-spec (loginAs('employee') → loginAs('manager')) is cheap every time, not just the first
- cy.session() resets the page to about:blank afterward — always pair it with an explicit cy.visit(); forgetting this is the most common first-time mistake
- The setup function can be a full UI login, not just an API call — the caching benefit is "pay the real cost exactly once, however expensive," not "you must use cy.request()." Essential for apps where no clean login API exists (SSO — see 7.4)
- vs Playwright: storageState is the same idea as an explicit, file-based artifact generated in a separate global-setup script — persists across separate CLI invocations (Cypress's cache does not, even with cacheAcrossSpecs), at the cost of more upfront wiring. vs Selenium: no equivalent whatsoever — session reuse is hand-rolled (manual cookie serialization) or, commonly, just not done, a real contributor to Selenium suites' reputation for being slow at scale

chapters.title: 7.3 Test Isolation & Reset-per-Test Behavior
chapters.overviewText: testIsolation: true (default since v12) clears cookies and Web Storage and navigates to about:blank before every it(). That is a page-state reset, not a browser relaunch. Pre-v12 cleared cookies but not localStorage. testIsolation: false is rare: sequential wizards or expensive read-only shared pages. Prefer one self-contained it() over splitting a journey and disabling isolation.
chapters.why: Order-dependent tests are among the most expensive bugs to diagnose. Enforced isolation makes that class structurally impossible. Disabling it costs it.only(), precondition guarantees, and sane retries.
chapters.when: When tempted to share login across it() blocks, when reading a pre-v12 tutorial that calls cy.clearLocalStorage() in beforeEach, or when an onboarding wizard is split into three tests.

practical.scenario: Three-step employee onboarding wizard, plus a slow annual payroll report with three read-only assertions.
practical.pass: You write one it('completes the full onboarding wizard'). You consider testIsolation: false only for the unchanging payroll report with a single before() seed.
practical.fail: You set testIsolation: false on the wizard so step 3 can it.only(), or you leave isolation on but still split the wizard and wonder why step 3 fails alone.

chapters.customSummary:
- testIsolation: true (default since v12), precisely: before every it(), Cypress clears cookies, clears localStorage/sessionStorage, and navigates to about:blank — which as a consequence wipes in-memory app state too. This is page-state reset, not a full browser-process relaunch (config, custom commands, and prior-test aliases aren't what's being reset here)
- Why this default is correct, not just strict: the alternative — tests silently depending on a previous test's leftover state — produces order-dependent failures that are exceptionally expensive to diagnose, because the symptom shows up in a test that reads as correct in isolation. Enforced isolation makes this bug class structurally impossible, trading a real performance cost (which 7.2 exists to recover) for a strong correctness guarantee
- Pre-v12 cleared cookies but NOT localStorage — a real historical gap that caused exactly this kind of silent cross-test pollution. Old tutorials' manual cy.clearLocalStorage() in beforeEach is now redundant, not wrong
- { testIsolation: false } — narrow legitimate use: genuinely sequential, order-dependent flows where continuity across steps IS the thing under test (a multi-page wizard), or expensive shared read-only setup across tests that don't mutate what they're reading (a reporting dashboard)
- Real costs of disabling it: loses independent runnability (it.only() on a later step fails without earlier steps), loses "each test proves its own precondition" (a silent bug in step 2 can corrupt step 3's result without step 2's own assertions catching it), and makes retry behavior order-dependent and harder to reason about
- The usually-better alternative to a sequential wizard block: don't split it into multiple it()s at all — write one self-contained test. Fully independently runnable, isolation stays on for the rest of the suite, and it honestly represents what it is: one continuous scenario. Treat { testIsolation: false } in a codebase as a flag worth questioning, not a default tool
- vs Playwright: philosophically identical — fresh BrowserContext per test() by default, with test.describe.serial() as the direct, named equivalent escape hatch and the same trade-offs. The convergence between the two tools here is a signal this reflects genuine testing best practice, not an arbitrary Cypress choice. vs Selenium: no isolation policy of any kind — structurally exposed to the order-dependency failure mode by default, avoided only through test-author discipline

chapters.title: 7.4 Handling Authentication
chapters.overviewText: UI login is for testing login itself (validation, lockout, MFA). Everything else uses programmatic login cached in cy.session(). Token apps set localStorage inside the session setup; cookie apps let cy.request() apply Set-Cookie. SSO: prefer a test-tenant grant; else cache a real cy.origin() UI login inside session; else stub the IdP. Logout tests must re-visit a protected route, not just check the URL.
chapters.why: A mature suite is not either/or. The canonical cy.loginAs(role) command is the payoff of Parts 6–7. SSO via cy.origin() inside session is the interview answer for Okta/Azure AD.
chapters.when: On day one of an HRM suite, when adding RBAC tests across employee/manager/admin, and when login redirects through login.okta.com.

practical.scenario: Login-form lockout tests, 80 leave tests needing a manager, Okta SSO, and payroll RBAC across three roles.
practical.pass: You UI-test only the login form; cy.loginAs uses session+validate+cacheAcrossSpecs; SSO setup wraps Okta in cy.origin inside session; RBAC switches roles cheaply.
practical.fail: You UI-login every leave test, skip logout's protected-route revisit, or try cy.request() against Okta's login page as if it were a password API.

chapters.customSummary:
- The core decision, and it's not either/or: UI login for testing the login mechanism itself (validation, lockout, MFA, "remember me"); programmatic login (cached via cy.session()) for every other test that merely requires an authenticated session as a precondition — the large majority of a real suite
- Canonical token-based pattern (brings together 6.1 + 7.1 + 7.2): cy.session(role, () => { cy.request POST /login → set localStorage }, { validate() {...}, cacheAcrossSpecs: true }), exposed as a typed cy.loginAs(role) custom command
- Cookie-based variant is simpler: no manual storage step needed, since cy.request() in the same browser context applies Set-Cookie automatically
- SSO/OAuth resists the clean shortcut because many identity providers deliberately offer no simple credential API. Three strategies in preference order: (1) a test-tenant / non-interactive grant if the provider offers one — functionally identical to the token pattern; (2) cache a real UI-driven SSO login inside cy.session(), using cy.origin() (Part 9.1) to cross into the identity-provider domain — still only pays the real cross-origin cost once per role per run; (3) stub the identity provider via cy.intercept() when realism can be traded for speed on the large majority of tests that don't care the handshake itself was faked
- Multi-role testing is made cheap by cy.session()'s per-role keying — switching identities mid-suite to test access control restores near-instantly each time, while still genuinely exercising distinct authenticated identities
- Logout deserves its own honest UI-driven test — and the strong version of that test doesn't just check the UI looks logged out, it re-visits a protected route afterward to confirm the app actually enforces the logged-out state, not merely displays it
- vs Playwright: identical strategic split, built on storageState; SSO handling is simpler — no cy.origin()-equivalent wrapper needed since Playwright was never origin-bound, so a global-setup SSO script reads as one continuous flow. vs Selenium: same UI-vs-programmatic split via a paired HTTP client and manual add_cookie() seeding, but no equivalent to cy.session()'s automatic caching-with-validation — teams hand-roll session reuse or simply accept paying full login cost per test
